group.passage:
Can you imagine what the Earth’s voice is like? The answer might go to the sounds of the didgeridoo, a long hollow wooden tube mainly used by the [[1]] people in Australia. In this country, there are over five hundred tribal communities, most of [[2]] have distinct languages and customs of their own. The didgeridoo, probably one of the world’s oldest musical instruments, has its origin from one of these tribes in Australia’s Northern Territory.
The traditional tribal instrument is primarily made of eucalyptus trees. The trunk is made into five-foot-long tubes in conical or cylindrical shape. The conical didgeridoos sound more dynamic and powerful; [[3]], the cylindrical ones convey soft and mellow sounds. Commonly performed at traditional rites like funerals, didgeridoos are normally not played as a solo instrument but as an accompaniment to chants and songs. Singers and dancers [[4]] while the didgeridoo player squats on the ground, resting the instrument on the earth. By blowing the tube with the technique “circular breathing,” which allows the sounds to last for long periods of time, the player produces an intermittent low-pitch drone. The low drone sounds of didgeridoos seem to be a [[5]] from the ground. If you listen closely, you might just hear the sounds of the wind, water, trees, and the whispers of the ancestors.

tags.topic: the didgeridoo, a traditional instrument of Aboriginal Australians
